name: Git
summary: The distributed version control system almost everyone uses: every clone holds the full history, stored as objects named by the hash of their content.
intro: At its core Git is a content-addressed object store, a key-value database where the key is a hash of the value. A file’s contents become a blob, a directory listing of blobs and subdirectories becomes a tree, and a commit records one top-level tree (a snapshot of the whole project), its parent commits, the author and the message. Each object is named by its hash, SHA-1 by default, so identical content is stored once and any corruption is detectable. Branches and tags are just refs: small names that point at a commit’s hash. New objects are written as individual compressed files; `git gc` later packs them into packfiles, storing similar objects as deltas of one another.

Because every clone has every object, nearly everything (commit, branch, merge, log, diff, blame) runs locally, and `git push` and `git fetch` only exchange the objects the other side lacks. Linus Torvalds wrote Git in April 2005 for the Linux kernel; Junio C Hamano has maintained it since July 2005, and it is a member project of the Software Freedom Conservancy, licensed under GPLv2 only. In Stack Overflow’s 2022 survey, 94% of respondents used it, and it underlies GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Azure Repos and AWS CodeCommit.

Git is in the middle of moving from SHA-1 to SHA-256. Since 2.13 (2017) it uses a SHA-1 variant that detects known collision attacks, and since 2.29 (2020) `git init --object-format=sha256` creates SHA-256 repositories, which can’t yet exchange objects with SHA-1 ones. The planned Git 3.0, which has no release date, will make SHA-256 the default for new repositories once forges and libraries support it, switch the default ref storage to reftable, name the first branch `main`, and require Rust to build. The latest release is 2.56.0 (September 2026).
strengths: Works offline: commits, branches, history and blame need no server, and every clone is a full backup
Branches are a pointer to a commit, so creating and switching them is nearly instant
Content hashes make history tamper-evident and deduplicate identical files
The common language of the industry: every major host, CI service and IDE speaks it
limits: Large binary files bloat every clone forever; use Git LFS or keep them out of the repository
Anything committed, secrets included, stays in the history until it is rewritten everywhere
Read access is per repository: anyone who can clone gets all of it, unlike Subversion’s per-path permissions
SHA-256 repositories can’t yet interoperate with SHA-1 ones, so most of the ecosystem still uses SHA-1

snippet.title: Look inside the object store
source: git cat-file -p HEAD            # tree <hash>, parent <hash>, author, message
git cat-file -p 'HEAD^{tree}'   # the snapshot: blobs and subtrees, each by hash
git count-objects -v            # loose objects versus packed ones
git gc                          # pack loose objects into a packfile
git init --object-format=sha256 new-repo   # a SHA-256 repository

sections.title: The four kinds of object
sections.intro: Everything in a repository’s history is one of these, named by the hash of its content.

items.name: Blob
items.text: The bytes of one file, with no name or permissions. Two files with the same contents anywhere in history share one blob.

items.name: Tree
items.text: A list of names, modes and the hashes of blobs and subtrees. A change deep in a directory creates new trees up to the root; unchanged subtrees are reused.

items.name: Commit
items.text: Points to one root tree, plus zero or more parent commits, the author and committer, and the message. Changing any of it changes the hash, and the hash of every later commit.

items.name: Tag
items.text: Like a commit for naming a release: a tagger, date, message and a pointer, usually to a commit. Lightweight tags skip the object and are just refs.

story: From 2002 the Linux kernel was developed in BitKeeper, a proprietary distributed version control system its maker let the community use free of charge. In April 2005 that relationship broke down. On April 6 Linus Torvalds told the kernel mailing list he would stop using BitKeeper and look for alternatives. He had hoped to switch only once there was a reasonable open-source alternative, and there wasn’t one.

He wrote his own. The first commit, on April 7, 2005, described “GIT, the stupid content tracker”: a content-addressable collection of objects named by their SHA-1 hash, with blobs and trees. On April 16 the kernel itself moved to Git, starting fresh from 2.6.12-rc2 rather than importing 3.2 GB of history. On July 26 Torvalds announced that Junio C Hamano was the new maintainer, and Git 1.0 followed in December.

GitHub opened in 2008, and Git went on to displace Subversion and CVS: in Stack Overflow’s 2022 survey, 94% of respondents used Git and 5% Subversion. Its later history is about keeping the design sound as it grew: Git 2.0 in 2014 changed long-standing defaults, a collision-detecting SHA-1 arrived in 2017 after the SHAttered attack, SHA-256 repositories in 2020, and optional Rust code in 2025.

choices.choice: Name every object by the hash of its content
choices.why: Torvalds wanted an object database where consistency could always be checked: if an object’s hash matches its content, the data is exactly what was stored. The same hashing deduplicates identical files and trees for free.

Earlier tools stored each file as a chain of changes. Git records the state of the whole project in every commit, which makes branching, merging and comparing any two points in history simple, with packfiles recovering the space through delta compression.

choices.choice: Speed and scale for the kernel first
choices.why: Speed and handling large projects like the Linux kernel efficiently were among Git’s original goals. Doing nearly every operation on the local disk, with no server round trip, was the way to get there.

Kernel development ran on patches mailed to maintainers, and Torvalds called “individual patches” a keyword. `git format-patch` and `git send-email` turn commits into emails, with the subject line as the email subject, and Git itself is still developed on a mailing list.

timeline.text: First commit April 7; the kernel moves April 16; Junio Hamano maintainer from July; 1.0 in December
Git 2.0, a release that deliberately breaks old defaults (May)
Git 2.13 makes collision-detecting SHA-1 the default after SHAttered
Git 2.28 makes the default branch name configurable; 2.29 adds SHA-256 repositories
Git 2.49 adds the first optional Rust code
Git 2.56.0 released September 28; Git 3.0 still has no release date
